name: Checks of widely repeated AI figures against their primary sources
description: Figures about AI that are often quoted, each checked against the source it is credited to, one row per claim. Each row gives the claim as it is usually repeated, the verdict, why, the sentence to cite instead, the sources and, where traced, how the claim travelled from its origin.
licence: Data: CC BY 4.0, Paweł Szczęsny, ai-first.company

rows.title: “30% of generative AI projects will be abandoned after proof of concept (Gartner)”
rows.claim: 30% of generative AI projects will be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, according to Gartner.
rows.summary: The figure is Gartner’s: a forecast, made in July 2024, that “at least 30%” of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025. Gartner published no method, sample or meaning of “abandoned”. Repeats drop “at least”, and many turn the forecast into a count or a failure rate. In January 2026 Gartner said that at least 50% had been abandoned: by its own account the forecast came true, but the 30% is out of date.
rows.correct: In July 2024, Gartner, which sells research and advice to IT leaders, predicted that “at least 30%” of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025. In January 2026, Gartner said that at least 50% had been abandoned, from its analysis of “hundreds of GenAI implementations”. Gartner published no method for either figure.
rows.scope: Generative AI projects stopped after a proof of concept, up to the end of 2025, as a lower limit. It is what Gartner expected in July 2024, not a count.

sources.label: Gartner (29 July 2024). Gartner Predicts 30% of Generative AI Projects Will Be Abandoned After Proof of Concept By End of 2025. Press release.
Chandrasekaran (26 January 2026). Why 50% of GenAI Projects Fail — And How to Beat the Odds. Gartner. Article with Gartner’s account of what happened by the end of 2025.
S&P Global Market Intelligence (30 May 2025). Generative AI experiences rapid adoption, but with mixed outcomes: Highlights from VotE: AI & Machine Learning. Summary of a paid survey report.

lineage.wording: At least 30% of generative AI (GenAI) projects will be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, due to poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs or unclear business value, according to Gartner, Inc.
lineage.change: Origin. A forecast credited to Gartner as a whole, released during a Gartner conference in Sydney. The release gives no method, no sample and no meaning of “abandoned”. The 30% is a lower limit (“at least”), but the release’s own headline drops “at least”.

lineage.wording: One-third of generative AI projects will be abandoned by 2025, Gartner says
lineage.change: In the headline, “At least 30%” becomes “One-third”. “After proof of concept” is dropped, so the forecast reads as if it covered all projects. “By the end of 2025” becomes “by 2025”. The body of the article quotes the release in full.

lineage.wording: 30% of genAI initiatives to fail in 2025 – Gartner
lineage.change: “Abandoned after proof of concept” becomes “fail”. “By the end of 2025” becomes “in 2025”. The headline drops “at least”. The article credits a report in AI Business, not Gartner’s release.

lineage.wording: Gartner finds that by the end of last year, at least 50% of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept due to poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs or unclear business value.
lineage.change: Follow-up. After the deadline, Gartner says “at least 50%” were abandoned. By Gartner’s own account, the forecast came true and was exceeded. The only method given: Gartner “analyzed hundreds of GenAI implementations”. No number of projects, dates or meaning of “abandoned” is published.

lineage.wording: GenAI rush begins; 30% of pilots abandoned post-POC (Gartner)
lineage.change: The forecast becomes a count, in the past tense, in a table row for 2024. “At least” is dropped, and “projects” become “pilots”. The next row, “Abandonment doubles to 42%”, joins it to a figure from an S&P Global survey of companies, which measured something else.

lineage.wording: Gartner analysts predicted that roughly 30% of GenAI projects would be abandoned after proof-of-concept by 2025. By early 2026, that estimate had climbed to at least 50% according to Gartner.
lineage.change: “At least 30%” becomes “roughly 30%”. Gartner’s 2026 statement that projects “were abandoned” is presented as a raised “estimate”. The forecast and the later figure now travel together.

rows.title: “66% of small businesses use AI”
rows.claim: 66% of small businesses use AI.
rows.summary: The figure is in the source, a 2026 online survey for the US Chamber of Commerce, a business lobby that argues against state AI laws in the same report. The report does not say how firms were recruited or weighted. Other US counts of the same kind of firm, made in other ways, are far lower.
rows.correct: In a 2026 online survey of US firms with fewer than 250 employees, run by Teneo Research for the US Chamber of Commerce, which campaigns against state AI laws, 66% said they used AI. Other US counts are lower: 46% of employer firms in the Federal Reserve Banks’ 2025 survey, 17.7% of firms that had paid an AI provider by the end of 2025 in Chase bank records, and under 20% of firms with four or fewer employees in the US Census Bureau’s survey.

sources.label: US Chamber of Commerce Technology Engagement Center and Teneo Research (2026). Empowering Small Business: The Impact of Technology on U.S. Small Business. Report.

rows.title: “70% of digital transformations fail (BCG and McKinsey)”
rows.claim: 70% of digital transformations fail, according to research by Boston Consulting Group and McKinsey. The same 70% is now quoted for AI transformations.
rows.summary: BCG did publish a 70% figure for digital transformations in 2020. It comes from executives’ own ratings and BCG’s client work, and it means “fall short of their objectives”: 44% of the transformations created some value. McKinsey published no 70% figure for digital transformations; its 70% lines, about change programmes and transformations in general, give no source. No source has measured how often AI transformations fail.
rows.correct: In a 2020 article, Boston Consulting Group, which sells transformation consulting, drew on its work with 70 client companies and a survey of 825 senior executives, who rated their companies’ digital transformations. By BCG’s measure, 30% met or exceeded their target value and produced lasting change, 44% created some value but missed their targets, and 26% created less than half of their target value. No source has measured how often AI transformations fail.
rows.scope: Digital transformations, as rated by 825 senior executives and seen in BCG’s work with 70 client companies, reported in October 2020. It does not hold for AI transformations or for change programmes in general.

sources.label: Forth, Reichert, de Laubier and Chakraborty (29 October 2020). Flipping the Odds of Digital Transformation Success. Boston Consulting Group.
Beer and Nohria (May–June 2000). Cracking the Code of Change. Harvard Business Review.

Garcia (29 March 2022). Common pitfalls in transformations: A conversation with Jon Garcia. McKinsey & Company.

lineage.who: Harvard Business Review (Michael Beer and Nitin Nohria)
lineage.wording: The brutal fact is that about 70% of all change initiatives fail.
lineage.change: Dead end. The figure is about “all change initiatives”, with no source, no count and no meaning of “fail”. A peer-reviewed review in 2011 found no valid and reliable evidence for a 70% failure rate of organizational change.

lineage.who: McKinsey & Company (Boris Ewenstein, Wesley Smith and Ashvin Sologar)
lineage.wording: We know, for example, that 70 percent of change programs fail to achieve their goals, largely due to employee resistance and lack of management support.
lineage.change: Dead end. McKinsey states the figure as known fact (“We know”) and adds two causes. No source or method is given. It is about change programmes, not digital transformations. A 2022 McKinsey interview repeats 70% for transformations in general, again with no source.

lineage.who: Boston Consulting Group (Patrick Forth, Tom Reichert, Romain de Laubier and Saibal Chakraborty)
lineage.wording: New BCG research shows that 70% of digital transformations fall short of their objectives, often with profound consequences.
lineage.change: Origin of the digital figure. 825 senior executives rated their transformations, and BCG added its work with 70 clients. The 70% is the 44% that created some value but missed targets, plus the 26% that created less than half. The subject becomes “digital transformations”, and the words are “fall short”.

lineage.wording: Research from Boston Consulting Group and McKinsey consistently shows that 70% of digital transformation initiatives fail to meet their objectives.
lineage.change: “Fall short of their objectives” becomes “fail to meet their objectives”, and the headline says “fail”. McKinsey is added as a second source. “Consistently” turns one 2020 result into a lasting pattern. The page is by a company that sells process management software.

lineage.who: Fortune (Julia Dhar, Kristy R. Ellmer and Philip Jameson)
lineage.wording: Corporate transformations fail much more often than they succeed. The failure rate is around 70% and this figure has not improved in decades.
lineage.change: Three BCG authors, writing in Fortune, give “around 70%” for corporate transformations in general. “Digital” is dropped. The figure is said to be unchanged for decades. No source is linked.

lineage.wording: 70% of enterprise AI transformations fail. Not because of the technology — because of the people. Here's the 5-pillar framework that separates the 30% who succeed from the 70% who don't.
lineage.change: “Digital transformations” becomes “enterprise AI transformations”. No source is given. The page is by a company that sells AI software, and it offers a framework for joining “the 30% who succeed”.

rows.title: “75% of knowledge workers use AI, and 78% bring their own tools (Microsoft)”
rows.claim: Three in four knowledge workers (75%) use AI at work, and 78% of them bring their own AI tools, according to Microsoft and LinkedIn’s Work Trend Index.
rows.summary: The claim matches the 2024 Work Trend Index by Microsoft, which sells AI tools for work, and LinkedIn, which Microsoft owns. The 75%, the 78% and its base, AI users, are as the report gives them. They are what 31,000 desk workers in 31 countries said in an online survey in February and March 2024. Each country counts equally in the 75%: the US figure was 71%, Japan’s 32%. Retellings go further than the report: they date the figures “now”, apply the 78% to all employees, and turn tools “not provided” by the employer into tools it “never approved”.
rows.correct: In an online survey of 31,000 desk workers in 31 countries, run in February and March 2024 for Microsoft, which sells AI tools for work, and LinkedIn, 75% said they used generative AI at work (71% in the United States). Of those users, 78% said they used AI tools their employer did not provide. A survey weighted to the whole US workforce found that 26.5% of US workers used generative AI at work in late 2024.
rows.scope: Desk workers in 31 countries who answered an online survey in February and March 2024, with each country counted equally. The 78% is a share of those who said they use generative AI, and counts tools the employer did not provide, not tools it banned.

lineage.who: Microsoft and LinkedIn, Work Trend Index
lineage.wording: Use of generative AI has nearly doubled in the last six months, with 75% of global knowledge workers using it. … 78% of AI users are bringing their own AI tools to work (BYOAI)—it’s even more common at small and medium-sized companies (80%).
lineage.change: Origin. Edelman Data & Intelligence surveyed 31,000 desk workers online, 1,000 in each of 31 countries, in February and March 2024, and pooled the answers. The 78% counts AI users whose tools were “not provided by their organization”. “Nearly doubled” comes from how long users said they had used AI.

lineage.wording: Microsoft’s 2024 Work Trend Index, released on Wednesday in partnership with LinkedIn, finds that, in the last six months, the use of generative AI has nearly doubled, with 75% of global knowledge workers using it. (Knowledge workers are considered professionals in roles like public accountants, engineers, editors, and lawyers.) In addition, 78% of AI users are actually bringing their own AI tools to the workplace, which is coined “BYOAI.”
lineage.change: The headline reads “Employees are secretly bringing their own AI tools to work”. The report itself framed the 78% as “keeping AI use under wraps”, but its question asked only who provided the tools. A definition of knowledge workers is added (“accountants, engineers, editors, and lawyers”) that is not in the report, which defines them as people who work at a desk.

lineage.wording: Nearly 80% of employees admit to using unapproved AI tools, exposing businesses to risk and wasted ROI
lineage.change: A second 78%, from a different survey. WalkMe, which sells software that guides staff through workplace tools, asked 1,000 US workers who already use AI. In its own body text, 78% said they use AI tools “not provided by their employer”. The headline turns that into “employees” using “unapproved” tools.

lineage.wording: According to Microsoft and LinkedIn’s 2024 Work Trend Index, 75% of knowledge workers now use generative AI at work, and 78% are using self-selected tools, commonly dubbed Bring Your Own AI (BYOAI) without organizational guidance.
lineage.change: “Of AI users” is dropped, so the 78% reads as a share of all knowledge workers. Data from early 2024 are “now” in late 2025. “Without organizational guidance” echoes the report’s own “without guidance or clearance from the top”; the survey question did not ask about guidance. The article presents it as “shadow AI”.

lineage.wording: About 78% of employees use AI tools their employer has never approved.
lineage.change: Dead end. No source is named; the page says only that the figure “comes from cross-industry usage research”. AI users become “employees”, and tools “not provided” become tools “never approved”. It could come from Microsoft’s survey or from WalkMe’s. The IT services firm’s article goes on to discuss a Microsoft product for finding unapproved AI.

rows.title: “77% of employees say AI has added to their workload (Upwork)”
rows.claim: 77% of employees say AI has added to their workload, according to a study by the Upwork Research Institute.
rows.summary: The 77% is in Upwork’s July 2024 report, but it is not about all employees. It counts workers who use AI and named at least one way AI had “decreased their productivity and added to their workload”, such as more time checking its output. Upwork’s own press release dropped “using AI”, and later articles said AI had “only” added work, or had not reduced it. The report does not say how many people this is, or whether AI also saved them time.
rows.correct: In a survey for Upwork, which runs a marketplace for hiring freelancers, workers in the US, UK, Australia and Canada were asked in April and May 2024 about AI at work. 77% of those who used AI named at least one way it had added to their workload or cut their productivity; the most common was more time reviewing AI-generated content (39%). The report does not say how many people answered this question, or whether AI also saved them time.
rows.scope: Workers who use AI, in a survey in the US, UK, Australia and Canada in April and May 2024, who picked at least one item from a list of ways AI added to their work. It does not show that AI made work heavier overall, or that 77% of all employees feel this.

lineage.wording: Over three in four (77%) say AI tools have decreased their productivity and added to their workload in at least one way.
lineage.change: Origin. Walr ran a survey of 2,500 people in four countries for Upwork in April and May 2024. The 77% counts workers who use AI and picked at least one listed burden, such as more time reviewing AI output (39%). The report does not say how many people answered.

lineage.wording: Data reveals 96% of C-suite leaders expect AI to boost worker productivity, but 77% of employees report AI has increased their workload
lineage.change: The sponsor’s own headline drops “using AI”, so the figure reads as all employees. “In at least one way” is dropped, so one listed burden becomes an “increased” workload. The body of the release keeps “employees using AI” once.

lineage.wording: 77 percent of 2,500 respondents said that AI had increased their workload even more - although the figures differed depending on people's position.
lineage.change: The 77% is put on all 2,500 respondents, who include 1,250 executives. “Even more” is added. Further down, the article says AI had “only added” to employees’ workload. heise cites a Forbes article that reported the press release.

lineage.wording: The Upwork Research Institute’s 2024 survey of 2,500 executives and employees found 77% of workers using AI said it added to their workload, not reduced it.
lineage.change: “Not reduced it” is added. The report does not say whether AI saved more time than it cost. “Decreased their productivity” and “in at least one way” are gone. The headline says “77% of workers”. The figure is repeated two years after the survey.

rows.title: “85% of AI projects fail (Gartner)”
rows.claim: 85% of AI projects fail, according to Gartner.
rows.summary: Gartner published an 85% figure about AI projects in February 2018. It was a forecast that “through 2022, 85 percent of AI projects will deliver erroneous outcomes due to bias”, not a count of failed projects. Repeats turned wrong results into failure and the forecast into a fact, and later added causes and dates that are in no Gartner text. The deadline passed in 2022, and Gartner has not published whether the forecast came true.
rows.correct: In February 2018, Gartner predicted that “through 2022, 85 percent of AI projects will deliver erroneous outcomes due to bias in data, algorithms or the teams responsible for managing them”. Gartner gave no method for this forecast, and it is not a count of failed projects. In Gartner’s own later surveys, respondents said that on average 54% (late 2021) and 48% (late 2023) of their AI projects made it into production, that is, into everyday use.
rows.scope: AI projects giving wrong results because of bias in data, algorithms or teams, up to 2022. It is what Gartner expected in February 2018, not a count.

lineage.wording: Gartner predicts that through 2022, 85 percent of AI projects will deliver erroneous outcomes due to bias in data, algorithms or the teams responsible for managing them.
lineage.change: Origin. Gartner forecasts that 85% of AI projects “will deliver erroneous outcomes due to bias”, for the years up to 2022. The release gives no method, no sample and no meaning of “erroneous outcomes”. It points Gartner clients to a paid report.

lineage.wording: Earlier this year, industry research firm Gartner made an audacious prediction: that 85 percent of AI projects won’t deliver for CIOs. That means in 20 artificial intelligence projects, only three will succeed – 17 of them will fall short.
lineage.change: “Will deliver erroneous outcomes due to bias” becomes “won’t deliver for CIOs”. Bias and the 2022 deadline are dropped. The headline adds “up to”, and a subheading asks why so many AI projects “fail”. The figure is still called a prediction.

lineage.wording: Last year, industry research firm Gartner made an audacious prediction: that 85 percent of AI projects don’t deliver. That means in 20 artificial intelligence projects, only three will succeed – 17 of them will fall short. With all the buzz and talk about AI technologies, that’s an interesting and surprising fact.
lineage.change: The text copies BMC’s paragraph almost word for word. “Won’t deliver” becomes “don’t deliver”, in the present tense. The prediction is called a “fact”. The panel’s title makes it “Why do ~85% of AI Projects Fail?”.

lineage.wording: Gartner pegs GenAI project failure at 85%, mostly from inadequate testing.
lineage.change: The figure becomes a failure rate of generative AI projects. The 2018 forecast was about AI projects in general. A cause is added: “inadequate testing”. No Gartner document is named or linked.

lineage.wording: 85% of AI project failures trace back to poor data quality. (Gartner, 2025)
lineage.change: The 85% becomes a share of failures, not of projects, and a cause is added: “poor data quality”. The figure is dated 2025 and linked to a Gartner statement of February 2025 that has no 85% figure.

rows.title: “95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing (MIT)”
rows.claim: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing, according to MIT.
rows.summary: The figure is in the report, but the report is preliminary and not representative. It rests on 52 interviews, 153 survey answers collected at conferences and a review of public announcements. Its authors call the figures “directionally accurate” rather than based on company reporting, and it defines success in two different ways.
rows.correct: A preliminary 2025 report from MIT’s Project NANDA, based on interviews at 52 organizations, 153 survey answers from senior leaders at industry conferences and a review of over 300 public AI initiatives, estimated that 5% of organizations had task-specific generative AI tools in production. The authors describe their figures as “directionally accurate based on individual interviews rather than official company reporting”.

sources.label: Challapally, Pease, Raskar and Chari (July 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025. MIT NANDA, preliminary findings. Copy of the report hosted by MLQ.ai.
Fortune (18 August 2025). MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing. The press coverage behind the claim.

rows.title: “AI could replace 300 million jobs (Goldman Sachs)”
rows.claim: AI could replace 300 million jobs worldwide, according to a report by Goldman Sachs.
rows.summary: The 300 million is in a March 2023 Goldman Sachs research note, but it measures something else. Goldman estimated how much work generative AI could technically do, and expressed it as the equivalent of 300 million full-time jobs “exposed” to automation. The same note expects only 7% of US jobs to be replaced, and most work to be helped by AI. “Expose” became “replace” in press reports within two days.
rows.correct: In March 2023, economists at the investment bank Goldman Sachs calculated from US and European data on job tasks that generative AI “could expose the equivalent of 300mn full-time jobs to automation” across large economies. That is an estimate of work AI could technically do, with no timeline. In the same note’s main case, 7% of current US jobs would be replaced by AI, 63% would be helped by it and 30% would be unaffected.
rows.scope: Work that generative AI could technically do across large economies, equal to 300 million full-time jobs, extrapolated from US and European task data in March 2023. It is a calculation with no timeline, not a count or a forecast of jobs lost.

lineage.who: Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research (Hatzius, Briggs, Kodnani and Pierdomenico)
lineage.wording: Extrapolating our estimates globally suggests that generative AI could expose the equivalent of 300mn full-time jobs to automation.
lineage.change: Origin. The authors scored the tasks of over 900 US occupations for what generative AI could do, extended the result to Europe and then to other large economies. The 300mn is a quantity of work, in full-time jobs, with no timeline. The next sentence says job losses have historically been offset by new jobs.

The first version of the headline said “in the US and Europe”, although the note extends the figure beyond them. The article itself keeps “exposing the equivalent of 300mn full-time workers across big economies to automation”.

lineage.wording: Artificial intelligence (AI) could replace the equivalent of 300 million full-time jobs, a report by investment bank Goldman Sachs says.
lineage.change: “Expose … to automation” becomes “replace”. The words “the equivalent of” and “full-time” stay. The article also says AI “may also mean new jobs and a productivity boom”.

lineage.wording: Report says AI could replace 300 million jobs worldwide. Is your livelihood at risk?
lineage.change: The headline drops “the equivalent of” and “full-time”, so a quantity of work becomes 300 million jobs. The article quotes the BBC (“as per BBC”), not the note.

lineage.wording: In fact, Goldman Sachs predicts that over 300 million jobs could be lost thanks to this fast-growing technology.
lineage.change: The estimate becomes a prediction of losses: “predicts that over 300 million jobs could be lost”. “300 million” becomes “over 300 million”. The headline says “AI will take over 300M jobs”.

lineage.wording: Innovation related to artificial intelligence (AI) could displace 6-7% of the US workforce if AI is widely adopted.
lineage.change: Follow-up. Goldman’s own later estimate of jobs lost is 6–7% of US workers, if AI is widely adopted, and 3% to 14% under other assumptions. The article expects the effect to be “transitory” as new jobs appear. It does not repeat the 300 million.

rows.title: “AI made customer support agents 14% more productive, and novices 34% (Stanford and MIT)”
rows.claim: Giving customer support agents an AI assistant made them 14% more productive, and novice and low-skilled agents 34% more productive, according to a study by Stanford and MIT.
rows.summary: The figures were measured from company records and appear in the authors’ November 2023 working paper. The peer-reviewed version, published in 2025, gives 15% on average and no figure for novices in its abstract. In the working paper, the 34% is for the fifth of agents with the weakest results before the assistant, not for the newest agents. The study covered chat technical support at one software company, with most agents working from the Philippines.
rows.correct: In a study of 5,172 customer-support agents at one Fortune 500 software company, most of them working from the Philippines, agents given an AI assistant resolved 15% more customer issues per hour on average (Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2025). Less experienced and lower-skilled agents gained the most. The most experienced and highest-skilled agents got slightly faster, and the quality of their work fell slightly.

rows.title: “AI will add $15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030 (PwC)”
rows.claim: AI will add $15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030, according to PwC.
rows.summary: The $15.7 trillion is in PwC’s 2017 report Sizing the prize, but as the most AI “could contribute” to world GDP in the single year 2030, compared with a world without AI, at 2016 prices. PwC wrote that its results are the potential “size of the economic prize”, not “direct estimates of future economic growth”. PwC’s own press release dropped “up to”, and the press turned “in 2030” into “by 2030”. More than half of the figure comes from consumers buying more, not from productivity.
rows.correct: In a 2017 report, the consultancy PwC, which sells AI services, calculated with an economic model that world GDP could be up to 14% higher in 2030 because of AI: the equivalent of $15.7 trillion in that year, at 2016 prices. PwC said this was the potential “size of the economic prize”, not a forecast of growth. Of the total, $9.1 trillion came from consumers buying more and better products, and $6.6 trillion from productivity.
rows.scope: The most AI could add to world GDP in the single year 2030, compared with a world without AI, at 2016 prices, as calculated by PwC’s model in 2017, before generative AI. It is a potential, not a forecast, and not a total over the years to 2030.

rows.title: “AI will affect 40% of jobs worldwide (IMF)”
rows.claim: AI will affect 40% of jobs around the world, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
rows.summary: The number and the source are right: a January 2024 IMF staff paper found that almost 40% of jobs worldwide are “exposed” to AI. Exposed means the occupation scores above the middle on a relative measure of how far AI’s abilities overlap with the job. The paper says this measure shows neither job losses nor gains, and leaves out how fast firms adopt AI. “Will affect” turns it into a prediction. The IMF’s own blog and speeches used that stronger wording.
rows.correct: An IMF staff paper from January 2024 (Cazzaniga and others) found that almost 40% of jobs worldwide, and about 60% in advanced economies, are in occupations with high “exposure” to AI: their tasks overlap more than the median with what AI can do. The authors say the measure is relative and static, and about half of the exposed jobs in advanced economies could benefit from AI. In October 2026 the IMF’s Managing Director wrote that it was “still too early to predict the toll on employment”.
rows.scope: The share of employment in occupations that score above the median on a relative AI exposure index, across 142 countries, with employment data from the ILO. It says which jobs AI’s abilities overlap with most, not how many jobs will change, or when.

rows.title: “AI will create 170 million jobs and displace 92 million by 2030 (World Economic Forum)”
rows.claim: AI will create 170 million new jobs and displace 92 million by 2030, a net gain of 78 million, according to the World Economic Forum.
rows.summary: The numbers are in the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025, but they are not about AI. They add up the job changes employers expect from all the trends they named: technology, the economy, demographics, the green transition and trade tensions. The report’s own figure for AI and information processing is 11 million jobs created and 9 million displaced. All of these figures are employers’ expectations, scaled up, not a count.
rows.correct: The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 asked over 1,000 large employers in mid-2024 how roles in their own organizations would change by 2030. Scaled up to about 1.2 billion formal jobs, their answers point to 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced, from all the trends they named together. For AI and information processing alone, the report expects 11 million jobs created and 9 million displaced.
rows.scope: Job changes from all the trends employers named together, across about 1.2 billion formal jobs worldwide, from 2025 to 2030. It is what large employers expected in 2024, scaled up, not a count.

rows.title: “Consultants using AI did 12.2% more tasks, 25% faster, with 40% higher quality (BCG and Harvard)”
rows.claim: Consultants using AI finished 12.2% more tasks, 25% faster, and produced 40% higher quality work, according to a study by Harvard and Boston Consulting Group (BCG).
rows.summary: The figures come from an experiment with BCG consultants assigned by chance to work with or without GPT-4. The repeated claim drops the condition the authors put in the same sentence: the gains are for 18 questions chosen because GPT-4 handled them well. On a task chosen because GPT-4 handled it badly, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less often right. The 40% is from the 2023 working paper; the peer-reviewed 2026 version reports 32%.
rows.correct: In a 2023 experiment, 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants were assigned by chance to work with or without GPT-4 (Dell’Acqua and colleagues, Organization Science, 2026). On 18 questions of one product-development exercise, chosen because GPT-4 handles them well, consultants using AI completed 12.2% more of the questions, reached the last question 25.1% faster and received grades on average 32% higher. On a business case chosen because GPT-4 gets it wrong, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to find the right answer.
rows.scope: 18 questions in one 90-minute product-development exercise, chosen because GPT-4 (as of April 2023) handled them well, done by about 385 BCG consultants. It does not hold for tasks AI does badly: on one such task, correct answers fell by 19 percentage points.

rows.title: “Copilot saves UK civil servants 26 minutes a day”
rows.claim: Microsoft 365 Copilot saves UK civil servants 26 minutes a day.

HMRC, with licences given at random, put the estimate at about an hour a week. The Department for Business and Trade found no evidence that time saved led to higher productivity.
rows.correct: In a UK government trial of Microsoft 365 Copilot with about 20,000 staff from October to December 2024, users estimated in a survey that it saved them 26 minutes a day on average. The figure is self-reported, and two departments that evaluated the tool separately found smaller or unproven gains.

rows.title: “Developers code 55% faster with GitHub Copilot (GitHub)”
rows.claim: Developers code 55% faster with GitHub Copilot, according to GitHub’s research.
rows.summary: The 55.8% is in a 2023 paper by researchers from GitHub, Microsoft and MIT, and it was measured: developers were timed in an experiment. But it is the time saved on one small programming task by 95 freelance developers hired online in 2022. Repeats turn it into how fast developers code in general and add “up to”. GitHub’s product page adds “without sacrifice to quality”, which the study did not test.
rows.correct: In an experiment run in May and June 2022 by researchers from GitHub, Microsoft and MIT, 95 freelance developers hired through Upwork were asked to write a small web server in JavaScript. Those given GitHub Copilot who finished took 71.17 minutes on average, against 160.89 minutes for those without it: a 55.8% cut in time. The study tested one task, and its authors say it “does not examine the effects of AI on code quality”.
rows.scope: One task, writing a small web server in JavaScript against tests given in advance, done by 95 freelance developers hired through Upwork in May and June 2022 with an early version of Copilot. It does not show gains in everyday work, on other tasks or in the quality of the code.

The authors describe these as “early, descriptive indicators” and not proof that AI caused the gap.
rows.scope: 22–25-year-olds in US payroll records from ADP, compared by how exposed their occupation is to AI. A relative gap that describes a pattern; the authors do not claim AI caused it. rows.title: “Generative AI saves workers 5.4% of their work hours (St. Louis Fed)”
rows.claim: Generative AI saves workers 5.4% of their work hours, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

It is what workers who had used generative AI the week before estimated it saved them, not time measured. Across all workers, including those who did not use it, the figure was 1.4%. Both figures are self-reported, and the authors’ revised paper of October 2025 puts the users’ figure at 5.2%.

rows.title: “Workers with AI skills earn a 56% wage premium (PwC)”
rows.claim: Workers with AI skills earn 56% more than those without them, according to PwC’s Global AI Jobs Barometer.
rows.summary: The 56% is in PwC’s 2025 Global AI Jobs Barometer, and the report’s own headline says workers with AI skills “command” it. But PwC compared the salaries offered in 2024 job ads, not what people are paid. An ad counted as needing AI skills when it listed at least one of 376 skills, most of them specialist machine-learning skills. Each edition gives a different figure: up to 25% in 2024, 56% in 2025 and 62% in 2026, which puts the year before at 57%.
rows.correct: PwC, which sells AI consulting and training, compared the salaries offered in job ads posted in 2024. Within the same occupation, ads that asked for at least one of 376 AI skills, most of them specialist machine-learning skills, offered on average 56% more than ads that did not (2025 Global AI Jobs Barometer). This compares advertised salaries, not what workers earn, and it does not show that AI skills cause the higher pay.
rows.scope: Salaries offered in job ads posted in 2024 (PwC’s data covers 24 countries, almost half of the ads from the US), for jobs that list at least one of 376 AI skills, compared with ads for the same occupation. It does not measure what workers are paid, or what using AI tools at work adds to pay.
